title: First Plasma
summary: Drive a repair robot inside a fusion reactor and set field probes, a null plate, a solenoid and a toroid so the first plasma holds.
subject: physics
concepts: Field of a long wire, B = μ₀I/2πr
Right-hand grip rule for the field direction
Field inside and outside a thick wire
Neutral point of two parallel currents
Solenoid B = μ₀nI, turns in all layers
Toroid B = μ₀NI/2πr, zero in the hole
learningOutcome: The student can use Ampère’s law to find the field of a long wire, inside and outside a thick wire, at a neutral point, in a solenoid and in a toroid.

levels.title: Calibrate the busbar probe
levels.adds: Baseline: B = μ₀I/2πr, with the field circling the wire by the right-hand grip rule (Ex 4.2, 4.3, 4.4).
hints: B = μ₀I/2πr = 2 × 10⁻⁷ I/r, with r in metres.
The field is at right angles to the line from the busbar to the probe.
Right-hand grip: thumb along the current, fingers curl the way the field goes.

levels.title: Inside the plasma
levels.adds: New idea: inside a column with a uniform current only the enclosed part counts, B = μ₀Ir/2πa², so one field occurs twice (Example 4.7).
hints: Outside, the Amperian circle encloses all of the current: B = μ₀I/2πr.
Inside, the circle encloses only I r²/a², so B grows in proportion to r.
The same field occurs once inside and once outside, and r_in × r_out = a².

levels.title: The X-point
levels.adds: More steps: superpose the fields of two currents and find where they cancel (Ex 4.4).
hints: Currents the same way cancel between them; opposite ways, only outside.
At the null the two fields are equal in size: I₁/x = I₂/(distance from current 2).
The null is always nearer the smaller current.

levels.title: Stretch the solenoid
levels.adds: New idea: inside a long solenoid B = μ₀nI, with n the turns per metre in all the layers (Ex 4.8, Example 4.8).
hints: Count the turns in all the layers, then divide by the length in metres.
B = μ₀nI, with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A. Give the field in mT.
The same turns spread over a longer coil give a weaker field.

levels.title: The toroidal field
levels.adds: Apply it: a toroid is a solenoid bent into a ring, B = μ₀NI/2πr in the winding and zero in the hole (beyond Section 4.7).
hints: A circle inside the winding encloses N turns of the current.
B = μ₀NI/2πr, so the field falls as 1/r across the winding.
A circle in the hole, or outside the ring, encloses no net current.

misconceptions: The field of a straight wire points along the wire
The field inside a current-carrying wire is zero everywhere
The field of a solenoid is strongest outside it
A toroid has a strong field in its hole
The neutral point of two currents lies midway between them
